summary: Notes from a 1969 conversation with Bob Kahn about how the ARPANET's message processor handles things such as character code conversion and the fields used between a host and its IMP. It records ideas and suggestions rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This short note records a conversation about how ARPANET computers could exchange text despite using different character codes. It also lists information that hosts and their IMPs might send to each other.

questions: what does rfc 6 say about character conversion
subtitle: A note recording a conversation about character conversion and Host-IMP communication.

tldr.problem: The conversation raises how the ARPANET should handle hosts that use different character codes and how hosts communicate with their IMPs.
tldr.mechanism: Steve Crocker records proposals discussed with Bob Kahn about character conversion, link fields and messages exchanged between hosts and IMPs.
tldr.outcome: The document is a record of a discussion, not a protocol specification.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 6 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document is a short note of a conversation dated 10 April 1969.

sections.title: Character-Code Conversion
sections.content:
The note says BB&N was prepared to convert character codes of 6, 7, 8 or 9 bits into 8-bit ASCII for transmission, then convert them again at the destination IMP. The proposed conversion used a one-for-one table unique to each host.

Crocker raises the possibility that hosts with 6-bit codes might need case shifting. Kahn notes that too many shifts could overflow; Crocker suggests that an overflow indication might be acceptable because he considers the case rare.
sections.plainLanguage: The discussion proposes translating different character codes into 8-bit ASCII for sending, then translating them again at the destination. It also considers what to do if changing letter case causes overflow.

sections.title: Host-IMP Fields and Conversion Control
sections.content:
For host-to-IMP communication, the note says there is a five-bit link field and a bit indicating conversion. It also discusses a possible two-bit conversion indicator: one bit for converting before sending and another for converting after sending.

The note suggests that the two-bit arrangement could provide another way to handle checking or controlling the system. It records this as a possibility in the conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: The host-IMP message has a link field and a conversion indicator. The speakers also consider using two conversion bits to give the system another way to check or control conversion.

sections.title: Information Hosts and IMPs Exchange
sections.content:
The note lists information a host can send to its IMP, including requests about tracing and conversion, whether a message is for a destination IMP or host, readiness for the next message, host status, synchronization, format errors, clearing a master link and requesting status.

It also lists information an IMP can send to its host: conversion information, arrival of a ready-for-next-message signal, IMP status, synchronization, a called host not responding, format errors and IMP status details.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can send its IMP control requests and ask for status. The IMP can report message readiness, host or IMP status, synchronization and errors.
